paragraphs: Nike signed rookie Chicago Bulls guard Michael Jordan in 1984 and released the first Air Jordan shoe the following year, designed by Peter Moore in the Bulls' red and black rather than the white a league dress rule at the time generally expected. The National Basketball Association fined Jordan for wearing them on court, a fine Nike reportedly agreed to cover, and the resulting publicity did the shoe far more good than harm.

The original Air Jordan sold well beyond expectations for a single athlete's shoe, and Nike kept releasing a new numbered model most years afterward regardless of whether Jordan still played. That lineage, combined with limited releases and resale markets, created the modern sneaker collecting culture, where value rests on scarcity and story as much as performance.

French engineer Louis Reard unveiled his two-piece swimsuit design at a Paris pool on 5 July 1946, just four days after the United States detonated an atomic bomb at Bikini Atoll in the Marshall Islands as part of its Operation Crossroads tests. No professional model would wear something so revealing in public, so Reard hired Micheline Bernardini, a dancer at the Casino de Paris, to model it instead.

He named the suit bikini to trade on the atoll's sudden fame, betting the design would cause the same shock the bomb test had. It worked as marketing, though the style took years to become mainstream: several countries banned it from public beaches, and the Vatican condemned it as sinful. Reard reportedly advertised that a true bikini should be small enough to pass through a wedding ring.

An eyed needle looks like a small thing to date a whole shift in human life around, but it marks the difference between draping a hide over the shoulders and cutting one to fit a body. Eyed needles turn up across Eurasia at different times, from around 40,000 years ago in Siberia to roughly 26,000 years ago in the layers this find belongs to in Europe.

Fitted clothing sewn with sinew or gut thread meant sealed seams, tighter cuffs and hoods, the kind of garment that let people stay outdoors through an ice age winter instead of sheltering through it. The needle itself, carved from a splinter of bone or antler and pierced with a hole barely wide enough for thread, is one of the plainest tools ever found and one of the most consequential.

The hatmakers Thomas and William Bowler built the first version in 1849 on commission from Lock and Co, the St James's hat shop, working from a design brief for Edward Coke, the younger brother of the Earl of Leicester. Coke wanted a close, hard hat for his gamekeepers at Holkham Hall, since their tall top hats kept getting knocked off, and sometimes damaged, by low branches while they rode.

When Coke collected the finished hat he is said to have tested its strength by stamping on it twice before agreeing to pay the twelve shillings asked for it. The close, domed shape proved practical well beyond the estate, and within a few decades it had become the standard hat of city clerks and businessmen across Britain, known there as the bowler after its makers and, confusingly, as the derby in the United States.

Thomas Burberry had invented gabardine, a tightly woven waterproofed cotton twill, in 1879, and by the outbreak of the First World War his firm adapted it into a coat British officers wore over their uniform in the flooded trenches of the Western Front. The coat had epaulettes for rank insignia, a storm flap across the chest, and D-rings at the belt meant for carrying kit, not decoration.

Because it was designed for the misery of trench warfare, the garment took its informal name, trench coat, from soldiers rather than from Burberry's marketing. After the war, veterans kept wearing the coats in civilian life, and its practical features, belted waist, deep collar, wide lapels, were absorbed into ordinary fashion through the interwar decades.

The dukes of Burgundy ran one of the wealthiest courts in fifteenth-century Europe, funded by trade wealth from the Low Countries, and used that money to set styles other courts then copied, including the tall, cone-shaped hennin headdress draped with a sheer veil that could reach a metre or more in height.

Men's fashion at the same court favoured short, padded doublets and long pointed shoes, paired with rich brocades woven with gold thread imported through the same trade networks that funded the court. The style spread through diplomatic and marriage ties across France, England and the Holy Roman Empire, making Burgundian dress, for a few decades, Europe's closest thing to an international fashion standard.

According to the historian Procopius, two monks who had spent years in China told the emperor Justinian that silk came not from a plant, as most Romans assumed, but from a worm, and offered to bring back the means to raise it themselves rather than keep buying finished thread through Persian middlemen.

They are said to have carried silkworm eggs out of China hidden inside hollow bamboo canes, travelling a northern route through Central Asia around 552. Whatever the exact details, a live domestic silk industry did take root in Byzantine territory soon after, breaking a Chinese monopoly that had lasted for centuries and letting Constantinople weave its own silk rather than trade for it.

The Greek geographer Strabo described continental Celts wearing chequered and striped woollen cloaks, and dye analysis of fragments recovered from Iron Age salt mines in Austria shows the same weavers using plant and insect dyes to build up multicoloured, banded patterns rather than plain fabric.

This is centuries before any specific tartan pattern was tied to a Scottish clan, a system that developed much later and mostly under commercial pressure in the 1800s. What the Iron Age evidence actually shows is a widespread European habit of checked woollen weaving, of which Scottish tartan is one late and heavily mythologised descendant rather than the origin.

Black had been reserved for mourning in Western fashion for generations, worn out of obligation rather than choice, which is what made Coco Chanel's plain black crepe dress, shown in 1926, a genuine break rather than just another design. It had a straight, unfussy cut and long sleeves, deliberately stripped of the beading and colour that signalled wealth in evening wear at the time.

American Vogue ran an illustration of it that October and reportedly called it a Ford, comparing its plain versatility to the mass-produced car available to anyone in one colour. The comparison was apt: Chanel had designed a dress that looked as good on a working woman as on someone wealthy, and the little black dress became a wardrobe category of its own rather than a single garment, still described in exactly those terms a century later.

Foot binding began among court dancers and elite women in the Song dynasty, working the toes under the sole and pulling the arch tightly with cloth wrappings, usually starting in early childhood before the bones had finished forming, so the shape it produced was permanent.

The practice spread from court circles down through the social scale over the following centuries, becoming tied to ideas of feminine refinement and, for many families, to marriageability itself, since a small, bound foot signalled that a woman did not need to do heavy field labour. It persisted for close to a thousand years, surviving repeated reform efforts, and was not effectively ended until campaigns in the early twentieth century.

Early corsets, sometimes called stays, were stiffened with strips of whalebone or reed sewn into channels of linen, laced tight enough to flatten and narrow the torso into whatever silhouette a given decade favoured, whether a rigid conical shape or a curved hourglass.

The style is often linked to Catherine de Medici at the French court, though the attribution rests on later tradition rather than firm contemporary record. What is well documented is how long the garment lasted: worn under most European women's clothing from the sixteenth century until well into the twentieth, it survived changes in fabric, fashion and politics that reshaped almost everything else about how people dressed.

Before 1856, a wide Victorian skirt was built up from layers of heavy petticoats, some stiffened with horsehair, adding weight and warmth nobody wanted. The steel cage crinoline patented that year replaced the padding with a light frame of flexible steel hoops connected by fabric tape, giving the same broad shape for far less weight.

The design spread fast because it was cheap to make and far more comfortable than what it replaced, and by the early 1860s cage crinolines were worn by women across Europe and North America regardless of class. Skirts caught in doorways, carriage wheels and open flames. The style shrank through the later 1860s into the narrower bustle that followed it.

Christian Dior showed his first collection under his own name in Paris on 12 February 1947, built around rounded shoulders, a tightly cinched waist and skirts so full they could use up to twenty metres of fabric, a wartime rationing figure that would have been illegal to use in France or Britain only two years earlier. Carmel Snow, editor of Harper's Bazaar, is credited with calling it the New Look after seeing the show, and the name stuck.

The collection was a deliberate return to an exaggerated hourglass silhouette after years of utility clothing cut to conserve cloth for the war effort. It was not universally welcomed: some British and American commentators criticised the fabric use so soon after rationing. The style nonetheless defined women's fashion for the following decade.

Kohl in ancient Egypt was ground from galena and other lead ores, mixed with fat or oil, and worn by men and women alike, not as a beauty product set apart from daily life but as something close to routine hygiene, applied from childhood.

Modern chemical analysis of residue in tomb containers has found lead compounds that do not occur naturally in galena, meaning Egyptians synthesised some ingredients through deliberate chemical processes. A 2010 study proposed that small doses may have boosted nitric oxide production in the skin, which could have helped fight eye infections common along the Nile.

Pleating linen without modern fabric finishes takes real effort: the cloth was dampened, folded or pressed over grooved boards, and left to dry so the creases held their shape through wear and washing, at least for a while, since the pleats had to be reset by hand each time the linen was laundered.

Tomb paintings and surviving fragments from the Old Kingdom show the fine, closely spaced pleating associated with elite dress, work fine enough that it demanded a servant or specialist launderer's time. Because linen this sheer and finely worked took skilled labour to produce and maintain, wearing it was itself a visible statement that someone else's labour was available to keep it that way.

Shaving the head in Egypt's climate was partly practical, cutting down on heat, sweat and lice, and wigs then let the same people present an elaborate head of hair without the daily upkeep a real one demanded. Surviving examples are built from human hair, sometimes reinforced with plant fibre, and dressed into tight curls or long plaits held with beeswax and resin.

Tomb paintings show wigged guests at banquets wearing small cones on top of their heads, once thought to be scented fat that melted and perfumed the wearer through the evening, though more recent excavation of actual burials has found solid cones that never melted at all, suggesting the imagery may be more symbolic than literal.

A ruff began as a simple drawstring frill at the shirt collar, but by the 1560s starch imported from the Low Countries let it stand alone as a separate garment, stiffened into rigid figure-of-eight pleats with a heated setting stick called a poking stick. The wider it grew, the less useful the wearer's arms became for ordinary work, which was the point: a ruff that size announced a household of servants to do the labouring.

Queen Elizabeth I's own portraits show ruffs widening across her reign, some later ones open at the front in a fan shape to display a jewelled bodice. Preachers and pamphleteers complained about the starch itself, since the yellowish tint some households favoured was rumoured to be set with saffron. The fashion collapsed after her death in 1603, as Jacobean collars fell open and flat.

The farthingale arrived in England from Spain, where it was called a verdugado after the willow or cane hoops, verdugos, sewn into channels of the underskirt. English tailors mangled the word into farthingale and by the mid-1500s were building two distinct shapes from it: a Spanish cone that tapered from waist to hem, and later an English drum farthingale that jutted straight out at the hip before falling vertically to the floor.

The drum shape needed a rigid wheel-like support called a bum roll or a wired frame worn at the hip, wide enough that a woman in full court dress sometimes had to turn sideways through a doorway. Elizabeth I's later portraits show the style at its most extreme. It fell out of fashion by the 1620s as softer, gathered skirts replaced the frame beneath them.

Spanish retailer Zara had already built its business around a short design-to-shelf cycle, sometimes weeks rather than a season, by watching what sold in its stores and rushing similar styles back onto the floor. As Zara and the Swedish chain H&M expanded internationally around 2000, that model, cheap runway-inspired clothing restocked constantly rather than in two seasonal drops, became the norm for large retailers.

The shift moved much of the world's clothing production toward factories in Bangladesh, China and elsewhere able to turn around small batches quickly and cheaply, training shoppers to expect new stock every week or two rather than twice a year. The same structure later drew criticism over garment worker conditions, following the 2013 Rana Plaza factory collapse in Bangladesh.

The fibers came out of Dzudzuana Cave in the foothills of the Caucasus, twisted from wild flax that nobody had domesticated. Radiocarbon placed them between roughly 34,000 and 27,000 years old, decades before agriculture, pottery or even the wheel existed anywhere.

What survives is not plain cord. Under microscopes the strands showed traces of black, grey, turquoise and pink, meaning someone had gone looking for colour on top of the plainer job of making thread. That single detail turned a scrap of ancient string into evidence of deliberate, decorative craft among people usually imagined only as hunters.

Flax had already been twisted into cord for tens of thousands of years by the time Neolithic farmers in the Near East began planting it deliberately and working the fibers on a loom rather than by hand alone. Growing the crop meant a supply that could be timed, retted and spun at scale, instead of gathered wild whenever a patch happened to be found.

Linen from this period does not survive in the ground the way stone or bone does, so the case rests on impressions left in clay, spindle whorls, and loom weights found at early farming sites. Woven cloth changed what a household could make and trade, turning a fiber crop into clothing, sails and eventually currency in its own right across the ancient Near East.

The corseted, floor-length silhouette that had defined women's fashion for a generation started breaking down during the First World War, when many women took factory and clerical jobs that a hobble skirt made impossible. By the early 1920s designers such as Coco Chanel and Jean Patou were cutting straight, low-waisted dresses that hung loosely from the shoulder rather than being shaped by a corset underneath.

The look took its name, flapper, from British slang for a young woman, and it came bundled with cropped hair, bared arms and hemlines that climbed to the knee by mid-decade, all treated at the time as a visible rejection of Victorian propriety. The style depended on jazz-era social changes as much as on cloth, since a dress built for dancing the Charleston needed to move in ways a corseted gown never could.

A chiton was not cut or fitted at all. It was a rectangle of linen or wool folded around the body and pinned at the shoulders with fibulae, then belted at the waist, which meant the same basic piece of cloth could be worn loose and short for working or draped long and full for formal occasions.

Because it required no tailoring, the chiton could be produced at home on a simple loom rather than bought from a specialist, and its drape became the standard the Greeks used to judge sculpture and dress alike for centuries. The heavier Doric version pinned along one open side, while the later Ionic style used more fabric and a row of pins or buttons down the arm, and both versions stayed in everyday use well into the classical period.

Persian cavalry had worn a raised heel for generations before this, a practical piece of riding equipment that let an archer brace in the stirrups while standing to shoot. In 1599 Shah Abbas I sent Persia's first diplomatic mission to the courts of Europe, seeking allies against the Ottomans, and European aristocrats who met the delegation took an enthusiastic interest in Persian style.

Heeled shoes spread through European courts afterward as a mark of status rather than horsemanship: a raised heel made walking or manual work harder, which was itself the point for people who wanted to show they did neither. Louis XIV later wore heels several inches high with the soles painted red, a style eventually restricted to those he personally permitted to wear it.

A houppelande used enormous quantities of cloth by design: a high collar, a fitted upper body, and then a skirt cut so wide and long that it had to be gathered into deep folds and belted, with sleeves that could hang down far past the wearer's hands and drag along the floor.

Both men and women wore versions of it at European courts, and the sheer yardage involved, sometimes embroidered, fur-lined or dagged along the hem into decorative points, made it a direct display of wealth rather than a practical garment. Because a houppelande consumed so much fabric, sumptuary laws of the period often singled it out specifically, restricting its length and lining by rank.

Cotton fibers and seeds from Mehrgarh, in what is now Pakistan, push cultivation back to around the same period the Indus Valley civilisation itself was taking shape, well before cotton is attested anywhere in the Mediterranean world or China.

What set the Indus apart was scale: sites such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa show cotton spinning organised as a proper craft, with dedicated tools rather than occasional household work. Greek writers a couple of thousand years later still described cotton as a strange plant that grew wool on trees, which is a fair measure of how long it took the rest of the ancient world to catch up with what South Asian spinners were already doing routinely.

Heian court dress before this point had followed Chinese cutting techniques closely, but Japanese tailors began using straight seams and rectangular panels instead, a change driven partly by practicality: straight-cut cloth is simpler to sew, easier to fold flat for storage, and adjusts to different bodies without refitting.

The result could be layered many times over for warmth or ceremony, most famously in the multilayered court robes worn by Heian noblewomen, where the visible edges of each layer were arranged to show a careful sequence of colours. That straight-cut structure barely changed over the following thousand years, which is why a garment shaped in the Heian period is still recognisably the same basic kimono worn today.

Jacob Davis was a Nevada tailor who kept getting requests from workers whose trouser pockets tore out under the strain of tools and mining gear. He started reinforcing the stress points with metal rivets, and the trousers held up well enough that he wanted to patent the idea, but lacked the money to file. He wrote to Levi Strauss, the San Francisco dry goods merchant who supplied him with denim cloth, and proposed they patent it together.

The two were granted United States patent number 139,121 on 20 May 1873, covering the riveted pocket construction rather than denim trousers as a whole, since work pants already existed. Strauss's company began manufacturing the riveted trousers under the name waist overalls, a term that stuck for decades before blue jeans became the common word for them in the twentieth century.

DuPont chemist Joseph Shivers led the team that developed a segmented polyurethane fibre able to stretch to several times its length and snap back to its original shape, work that grew out of the same Delaware labs that had produced nylon decades earlier. DuPont announced the fibre in 1958 and brought it to market in 1962 as Lycra, though the generic term spandex, an anagram of expands, became the more common name.

The fibre found its first major market in girdles and foundation garments, offering the same shaping effect as older rigid corsetry without any boning at all. It moved into swimwear and sportswear through the 1960s and 1970s and became essential to activewear more broadly once stretch fabric blends made close, flexible-fitting clothing practical for exercise rather than only for display.

Charles Macintosh was a Glasgow chemist who had been experimenting with the waste naphtha left over from gasworks when he found it could dissolve rubber into a liquid that stayed flexible. In 1823 he patented a way of sandwiching that rubber solution between two layers of wool cloth, which sealed the fabric without the previous problem of rubber going stiff in cold weather and sticky in heat.

The early coats still had drawbacks: seams could leak, and the rubber layer softened uncomfortably in strong summer sun. Macintosh partnered with the Manchester firm of Thomas Hancock, whose own rubber-processing improvements helped make the garment reliable enough to sell widely. The brand name stuck to the whole category, and mac or mackintosh is still the everyday British word for a raincoat two centuries later.

The pouf was built on a wire and horsehair frame, padded out and dressed over the wearer's own hair, sometimes raised so high a woman had to kneel on the carriage floor to fit inside it. Marie Antoinette's hairdresser Leonard Autie and the milliner Rose Bertin turned the style into a running commentary on events, building poufs shaped like ships, gardens or windmills.

One version, the pouf a l'inoculation, celebrated the queen's support for smallpox inoculation by working a serpent and an olive branch into the design. The style needed frequent attention from a live-in hairdresser and could not be washed easily, so lice and vermin in a pouf were a recognised hazard of court life. It faded after the Revolution began in 1789, when elaborate court fashion itself became dangerous to display.

Poulaines stretched the toe of a shoe far beyond the foot inside it, sometimes stiffened with whalebone or stuffed with moss to hold the point rigid, a shape that made walking any real distance genuinely awkward and therefore useful as a display of exactly that: a wearer who did not need to walk far or work with their hands.

The style grew so extreme in places that English and French authorities passed sumptuary laws capping toe length by rank, since only nobles were meant to afford the impracticality. Some accounts describe points long enough that wearers tied them to their knees or shins with cord to keep from tripping, and clerics of the period condemned the fashion as vain and even indecent.

Mary Quant ran a boutique called Bazaar on London's King's Road from the late 1950s, and by the mid-1960s she was selling skirts cut several inches above the knee, a length she said she named after her favourite car, the Mini. She later said the length itself was driven by her young customers, who kept asking for hemlines shorter than what she was already selling.

The style spread fast through swinging London and then internationally, helped by models such as Twiggy and by newspaper coverage that treated the hemline as a genuine controversy. French designer Andre Courreges also claimed credit for the innovation around the same period, but it was Quant's version, sold cheaply and in volume from her own shop, that made the miniskirt an everyday garment.

Mary Phelps Jacob, a young New York socialite, wanted something under a sheer evening gown that would not show the whalebone ridges of a corset. In 1913 she had her maid sew together two silk handkerchiefs and a length of pink ribbon, and the improvised garment worked well enough that friends started asking her to make copies for them.

She filed for a patent under the name Caresse Crosby in February 1914 and was granted United States patent number 1,115,674 that November for a backless brassiere, built without the rigid boning that had defined women's underwear for decades. She tried running a small manufacturing company but had little head for business, and within a couple of years sold the patent to the Warner Brothers Corset Company for fifteen hundred dollars.

Croatian soldiers serving in French royal regiments during the Thirty Years' War wore a knotted neckcloth as part of their uniform, and Parisians who saw them passing through in the 1630s and 1640s started calling the style a la croate, a phrase that wore down over time into cravate. Louis XIV, who came to the throne as a child in 1643, grew up seeing it at court and adopted it himself, which was enough to make it fashionable across Europe.

By the 1660s the cravat had become a marker of rank rather than a soldier's practical neckcloth, tied in lace or fine linen and sometimes finished with a ribbon bow called a Steinkirk after a later battle. The word survives almost unchanged in French and Croatian both, and it is the direct ancestor of the knotted necktie.

DuPont chemist Wallace Carothers had developed nylon in the mid-1930s as a synthetic silk substitute, and the company chose stockings as the product to prove it commercially viable. Nylon stockings went on sale in select American stores starting 15 May 1940, and some accounts describe shops in New York and other cities selling out within hours as women queued for a fibre that did not run or sag like silk.

Roughly sixty-four million pairs sold in the first year alone. The supply dried up almost as fast once the United States entered the war in December 1941, since DuPont redirected nylon production toward parachutes and other military uses, and the resulting shortage led some women to paint a seam line up the back of bare legs to fake the look until stockings returned to shelves after 1945.

Otzi did not die in a single outfit by accident of preservation; he died wearing layers built for altitude. His leggings were stitched leather, his coat pieced together from goat and sheep hide, and his cap sewn from brown bear fur, each layer chosen for a different animal's particular warmth or wear resistance.

His shoes were the most inventive piece: an inner net of bark string stuffed with hay for insulation, wrapped in a bearskin sole and deerhide upper. Nothing about the outfit reads as ceremonial. It is a working wardrobe from around 3300 BCE, assembled by someone who needed to survive the Alps and froze there before he could replace any of it.

Panniers took the farthingale's old trick of hoops under fabric and turned it sideways: instead of a skirt jutting out evenly all around, two separate cane or whalebone frames sat at each hip, so a court dress could be several feet wide from side to side while staying nearly flat front to back. That shape let a woman pass through a normal doorway by turning sideways, which a true drum farthingale could not manage.

By the 1740s French court panniers, sometimes called hoop petticoats, had grown wide enough that some versions hinged so the wearer could fold them up briefly to get through a narrow space or into a carriage. The width became a canvas for embroidery, and the most extreme court versions survived in France into the 1780s even after everyday fashion had already moved to softer, narrower skirts.

Louis XIV started losing his hair young, and by his twenties in the 1660s he was covering the thinning patches with an elaborate wig rather than admit to it. Because nobody at Versailles was going to appear better groomed than the king, wigs became mandatory at court almost overnight, and the fashion for men's wigs spread out from France across Europe within a decade.

The powder itself, usually scented starch, was applied fresh before an appearance and made a mess wherever it went, which is part of why dedicated powder rooms became a feature of grand houses. A large wig also signalled that its wearer did not do manual work and could afford a servant to dress it. The style lasted through most of the eighteenth century before wig taxes and simpler Regency fashions ended it.

Before buttons or zips existed, a fibula did the job a safety pin does now: a pin with a coiled spring at one end and a catch plate at the other, closing a loop of cloth at the shoulder or chest and holding it there under tension rather than by friction alone.

Romans inherited the design rather than inventing it, adapting earlier Greek and Etruscan pins, but they mass-produced fibulae in bronze and iron across the empire and dressed them up in silver, enamel and gemstones for wealthier wearers. Because styles shifted with fashion and region, archaeologists now use fibula designs almost like pottery styles, to date and place Roman-era graves and settlements.

Caligae were open, sandal-like boots built from several layers of thick leather stitched together, with straps that laced up the front and left the toes exposed, a design suited to marching long distances in a variety of climates without the foot overheating inside a closed boot.

Their soles were studded with iron hobnails, which gave grip on stone roads and extended the wear of the leather, but which also made caligae genuinely dangerous on smooth or icy ground, something ancient sources note as a real hazard rather than a footnote. The emperor Caligula got his nickname, meaning roughly little soldier's boot, as a child from wearing a miniature pair among his father's troops.

The Lex Oppia, passed during the pressure of the war against Hannibal, capped how much gold women could own and restricted brightly dyed clothing, framed at the time as wartime austerity rather than fashion policing. It became one of Rome's most contested laws: two decades later, once the war was won, women reportedly demonstrated in the streets to have it repealed.

Later Roman sumptuary laws went further, restricting who could wear purple dye at all and tying particular colours and fabrics to specific ranks and offices. The pattern recurs across the ancient and medieval world: clothing regulated by law almost always turns out to be regulating status and gender as much as spending, with luxury dress serving as a visible marker lawmakers wanted kept under control.

A toga was a single, semicircular piece of wool several metres across, wound and draped over a tunic without a single pin or clasp holding it shut. Getting it to sit correctly took practice, and wealthier Romans often had a household slave help arrange the folds each morning before leaving the house.

Its plainness or colour marked exact legal standing: a plain white toga virilis for an ordinary adult male citizen, a purple-bordered toga praetexta for magistrates and boys not yet of age, and an all-purple version reserved for a general celebrating a triumph. Women, slaves and foreigners could not wear one at all, which made the toga less a fashion item than a piece of civic identification worn on the body.

Rubber-soled canvas shoes existed in various forms from the mid-1800s once Charles Goodyear's vulcanisation process made rubber durable enough for footwear, but they stayed a niche item for tennis and croquet, played on lawns a hard leather sole would tear. The soft sole also let the wearer move almost silently across a wooden floor, which is where the word sneaker came from, since a policeman could not hear one coming.

By the 1890s manufacturers on both sides of the Atlantic were producing them at scale for a growing leisure and sporting goods market, well before the Keds brand formalised the category name in the 1910s. The shoe's appeal was less about style at first than about grip and quiet, and it took basketball and, much later, street fashion to turn the sneaker into the everyday object it became.

A heel narrow enough to be called a stiletto, after the thin dagger, needed a technical breakthrough as much as a design one: earlier slim heels split or snapped under a walking stride, and it took a steel or metal rod inserted through the heel's core, developed by shoemakers including Roger Vivier working for Christian Dior in the early 1950s, to make a heel that thin able to bear a person's weight.

Vivier's needle-thin heels for Dior's collections through 1954 and after are usually credited as the design that made the stiletto commercially viable rather than a novelty, and Italian makers of the same period pushed the shape further. The heel concentrated a woman's entire weight onto a point smaller than a coin, which is exactly why it became shorthand for glamour: it was visibly impractical, and that was the appeal.

Charles II announced at his court in October 1666 that he intended to set an example of thrift after the plague and the Great Fire, wearing a plain, fixed style of dress rather than the changeable French fashions of the day. The outfit he described to his courtiers was a long coat, a knee-length vest worn underneath it, and breeches, giving England a native alternative to imported French style.

Samuel Pepys recorded the king wearing the new vest in his diary that October, noting the whole court had turned out in the style within days. The combination of coat, waistcoat and breeches did not stay fixed exactly as Charles specified, but the three-part structure held, evolving over the following century into the matched three-piece suit that remained the standard shape of formal male dress into the twentieth century.

London hatter John Hetherington is said to have caused a small riot when he first wore a tall, silk-covered top hat in public in January 1797, with newspaper accounts claiming women fainted and a boy broke his arm in the crowd it drew, though how much of that story is embellishment rather than fact is hard to pin down at this remove. The shape itself grew out of the earlier, shorter beaver-felt hats worn through the eighteenth century.

Whatever the truth of Hetherington's debut, the tall hat caught on quickly and by the early 1800s had become the standard formal headwear for men across Europe, worn with everything from a morning coat to full court dress. It stayed dominant through most of the nineteenth century before the bowler and later the trilby offered less formal, more practical alternatives for everyday wear.

Howard Carter found the sandals on the pharaoh's actual feet when the wrappings around the mummy were unwrapped in the 1920s, gold soles curled slightly upward at the toe and finished with a design of bound captives underfoot, so that every royal step was, in image at least, taken on the necks of Egypt's enemies.

Tutankhamun died young, likely in his late teens, and the sheer volume of gold, inlay and jewelled regalia packed into his comparatively modest tomb has long puzzled Egyptologists, since better-documented pharaohs with grander tombs were stripped by looters within centuries. His survived largely intact, which is the accident of history that let a boy king's footwear become the best-known royal sandals from the ancient world.

Making the dye meant crushing or gutting thousands of sea snails from the Murex family for their mucous gland alone, then fermenting that gland in vats of salt water for days until it broke down into a compound that turned purple only once exposed again to air and light. One estimate puts the yield at roughly 12,000 snails for barely more than a gram of usable dye.

The smell of the vats was strong enough that Phoenician dyeing works were kept downwind of their own towns, yet the colour that came out of them barely faded, which was rare among ancient dyes and part of why it held its value. Named for the Phoenician port of Tyre and traded across the Mediterranean, it stayed expensive enough that later Roman and Byzantine law simply reserved it for emperors.

Umbrellas were already common for women in London by the early 1700s, but a man carrying one was considered effeminate and a plain insult to the city's hackney coachmen, who made their living off people sheltering from rain. Jonas Hanway, a traveller and philanthropist who had picked up the habit in Paris, began carrying one openly through London streets around 1750 anyway, and was reportedly jeered and pelted for it.

Hanway kept doing it for roughly thirty years until his death in 1786, by which point enough other men had followed him that the ridicule had mostly stopped. He is remembered today less for founding the Magdalen Hospital for young women, his actual life's work, than for being the man credited with making it socially acceptable for an Englishman to walk down the street holding an umbrella.

Swiss engineer George de Mestral picked burdock burrs off his clothes and his dog's fur after a walk in the Alps sometime in the 1940s and examined them under a microscope, finding that each burr was covered in tiny hooks that snagged on the loops of fabric or fur. He spent years working out how to reproduce that mechanism in nylon, since the material needed to hold its shape under heat when the hooks were cut.

De Mestral filed his Swiss patent in 1951 and received the equivalent United States patent in 1955, naming the product Velcro, a blend of the French words velours and crochet, meaning velvet and hook. The fastener was slow to catch on commercially until NASA adopted it for use in spacesuits and equipment in the 1960s, after which it spread into ordinary clothing, shoes and countless household products.

The carvings themselves have no faces. Whoever shaped these small limestone and ivory figures across ice age Europe spent their detail instead on the head and hips: rows of carved lines that archaeologists read as woven caps or braided hairstyles, and a string skirt hanging in strands from the waist.

No actual textile from this far back survives to compare against the stone, so the figurines are read as the earliest picture, rather than the earliest fabric, of clothing meant to decorate rather than only cover. A string skirt keeps nobody warm; its rows of cord swing and click when the wearer moves, which is why some archaeologists treat it as a signal of status or fertility rather than a functional garment.

A single Viking sail could take one woman a year or more of spinning and weaving to produce, and a longship needed both a sail and a full set of clothing for its crew, so wool production was not a side task in a Norse household but one of its largest ongoing jobs, organised around the seasons of shearing, spinning and weaving.

Men typically wore wool tunics and trousers under a cloak fastened with a brooch, while women wore a long wool or linen underdress topped by a pinafore-style overdress held up with straps and oval brooches, a style distinctive enough that archaeologists use surviving brooch pairs to identify Norse graves. The same fiber that clothed a household also, woven differently, caught the wind that carried Viking ships across the North Atlantic.

Wild sheep do not grow fleece worth shearing. Their coats are a coarse outer hair over a thin undercoat, and it took generations of selective breeding after domestication for that undercoat to thicken into the soft, continuous wool that could be pulled and spun into thread.

Once herders had that woolly fleece, they gained something flax could not offer: a fiber that regrew every year on a living animal, needed no field and no harvest, and could be dyed and felted more easily than linen. Early spindle whorls and loom weights from Mesopotamian and Iranian sites mark wool's spread as clothing, not just as a curiosity of animal breeding.
